title: Right Triangle Trigonometry
concept: Three ratios — SOH-CAH-TOA — define every right-triangle trig problem on the SAT. Sin(θ) = opposite/hypotenuse. Cos(θ) = adjacent/hypotenuse. Tan(θ) = opposite/adjacent. The two sides are always relative to the angle you are working with: opposite is across from θ, adjacent is the leg touching θ (but not the hypotenuse), and hypotenuse is always the longest side across from the right angle. A fourth fact cuts many problems in half: sin(θ) = cos(90° − θ), because the two acute angles of a right triangle are complementary. To find a missing side, multiply the hypotenuse by the trig ratio (or divide, if the hypotenuse is what you want). Desmos defaults to degrees and can evaluate any trig expression instantly — type sin(30)*20 and press Enter.

workedExamples.problem: A 20-foot ladder leans against a wall at a 30° angle with the ground. How high up the wall does it reach?
steps: Label the sides: the ladder is the hypotenuse (20 ft), the height is opposite the 30° angle.
SOH: sin(30°) = opposite/hypotenuse → opposite = hypotenuse × sin(30°).
sin(30°) = 0.5 (special angle — memorize or use Desmos: type sin(30)).

workedExamples.problem: In a right triangle with legs 3 and 4 and hypotenuse 5, what is cos of the angle θ adjacent to the leg of length 4?
steps: The side adjacent to θ (not the hypotenuse) is 4. The hypotenuse is 5.
No calculator needed — simplify the fraction directly.

trapPatterns: sin_cos_swap: using sin when cos is needed (or vice versa) — the most common error. Always re-label the sides relative to the specific angle in the problem before picking a ratio.
inverted_ratio: dividing instead of multiplying when finding a side — e.g. computing 20 ÷ sin(30°) = 40 instead of 20 × sin(30°) = 10. Only divide when the hypotenuse is the unknown.
used_wrong_reference_angle: computing trig from the wrong angle — in triangle ABC the adjacent and opposite sides swap when you move from angle A to angle C.
forgot_to_multiply: setting up the correct ratio correctly on paper but forgetting the multiplication step and reporting the hypotenuse as the answer.
tan_vs_sin: using tan = opposite/adjacent when sin = opposite/hypotenuse is needed, because both ratios involve the opposite side.
calculatorStrategy: use_desmos_graph — type the trig expression directly into Desmos (e.g. sin(30)*20) for instant numeric results. Desmos defaults to degrees; no mode change needed. For ratio-from-sides problems (given both legs/hypotenuse), no calculator is required — simplify the fraction.

problems.calculatorStrategy: use_desmos_graph — the ratio simplifies to a fraction; no calculator needed here. In Desmos you could type 3/5 to confirm.
problems.question: A loading dock ramp has a rise of 3 feet, a horizontal run of 4 feet, and a ramp length of 5 feet. What is the value of sin(θ), where θ is the angle the ramp makes with the ground?

choices.label: B
choices.trap: sin_cos_swap: used adjacent/hypotenuse (cos θ) instead of opposite/hypotenuse (sin θ).

choices.label: C
choices.trap: tan_vs_sin: used opposite/adjacent (tan θ) instead of opposite/hypotenuse.

choices.label: D
choices.trap: inverted_ratio: flipped the ratio to hypotenuse/opposite.

explanation: SOH: sin = opposite/hypotenuse.
The side opposite θ (the angle at ground level) is the rise = 3. The hypotenuse (ramp length) = 5.
Trap B (4/5): 4/5 is cos(θ) — you used adjacent/hypotenuse, not opposite/hypotenuse.
Trap C (3/4): 3/4 is tan(θ) — opposite/adjacent, not opposite/hypotenuse.
Trap D (5/3): the ratio is inverted.
Desmos check: type 3/5 → 0.6. ✓

problems.calculatorStrategy: use_desmos_graph — type sin(30)*20 into Desmos. Desmos defaults to degrees; answer appears instantly.
problems.question: A 20-foot ladder leans against a vertical wall. The ladder makes a 30° angle with the ground. Using sin(30°) = 0.5, how high up the wall does the ladder reach, in feet?
explanation: The ladder is the hypotenuse (20 ft). The wall height is the side opposite the 30° angle.
SOH: sin(30°) = opposite/hypotenuse → opposite = hypotenuse × sin(30°).
Height = 20 × 0.5 = 10 feet.
Trap: 20 (full ladder length — forgot to multiply by sin).
Trap: 40 (divided instead of multiplied: 20 ÷ 0.5 = 40).
Desmos: type sin(30)*20 → 10. ✓

problems.calculatorStrategy: use_desmos_graph — not needed here; this is pure angle arithmetic (90 − 38). Desmos can confirm: type cos(38) and sin(52) and verify they match.
problems.question: A kite string makes a 38° angle with the ground. If sin(38°) = cos(x°), what is the value of x?

choices.label: B
choices.trap: used_wrong_reference_angle: assumed cos(x°) = cos(38°), so x = 38 — ignored the complementary identity.

explanation: The complementary angle identity: sin(θ) = cos(90° − θ) for any acute angle θ.
The two acute angles in a right triangle always add to 90°.
Trap B (38): sin(θ) ≠ cos(θ) in general — that's only true at 45°.
Trap C (128): 90 + 38 goes the wrong direction.
Trap D (142): 180 − 38 is the supplementary angle, not the complementary one.
Desmos: type sin(38) and cos(52) side by side — both return the same value. ✓

problems.calculatorStrategy: use_desmos_graph — type (3/5)*50 into Desmos for the multiplication. Or note sin(θ)=3/5=0.6, so 50×0.6=30 mentally.
problems.question: A kite is attached to a 50-foot string. The string makes an angle θ with the ground where sin(θ) = 3/5. How high above the ground is the kite, in feet?

choices.label: B
choices.trap: sin_cos_swap: used cos(θ) = 4/5 instead of sin(θ) = 3/5 → 50 × (4/5) = 40.

choices.label: C
choices.trap: forgot_to_multiply: reported the full string length instead of multiplying by sin(θ).

choices.label: D
choices.trap: inverted_ratio: divided 50 ÷ (3/5) = 83.3 ≈ 83, using hypotenuse-finding formula when a leg was wanted.

explanation: The string is the hypotenuse (50 ft). The height of the kite is the side opposite θ.
SOH: sin(θ) = opposite/hypotenuse → opposite = hypotenuse × sin(θ).
Height = 50 × (3/5) = 30 feet.
Trap B (40): 4/5 is cos(θ) — you swapped sin and cos.
Trap C (50): you forgot to multiply; the full string length is the hypotenuse, not the height.
Trap D (83): dividing by sin finds the hypotenuse; you already have the hypotenuse and want the leg.
Desmos: type (3/5)*50 → 30. ✓

problems.calculatorStrategy: use_desmos_graph — not needed; simplify 4/5 directly from the sides. Desmos can confirm: type 4/5 → 0.8.
problems.question: A 5-foot ladder leans against a wall and reaches exactly 3 feet up the wall. The ladder makes an acute angle θ with the ground. What is the value of cos(θ)?
explanation: The ladder is the hypotenuse (5 ft). The wall height (3 ft) is the side opposite θ.
First find the adjacent side (horizontal distance from wall to base of ladder): by the Pythagorean theorem, adjacent = √(5² − 3²) = √(25 − 9) = √16 = 4.
CAH: cos(θ) = adjacent/hypotenuse = 4/5.
This is a 3-4-5 right triangle — the adjacent leg is 4.
Trap 3/5: that is sin(θ) = opposite/hypotenuse, not cos.
Trap 5/4: the ratio is inverted.
Desmos: type 4/5 → 0.8, or arccos(4/5) to verify the angle. ✓

problems.calculatorStrategy: use_desmos_graph — type cos(60)*16 into Desmos. cos(60°)=0.5, so 16×0.5=8.
problems.question: A wheelchair ramp is 16 feet long and makes a 60° angle with the ground. Using cos(60°) = 0.5, what is the horizontal distance the ramp covers, in feet?

choices.label: B
choices.trap: forgot_to_multiply: reported the full ramp length instead of multiplying by cos(60°).

choices.label: C
choices.trap: inverted_ratio: divided the ramp length by cos(60°): 16 ÷ 0.5 = 32, which finds the hypotenuse when hypotenuse is unknown.

choices.label: D
choices.trap: sin_cos_swap: used sin(60°) ≈ 0.866 instead of cos(60°) = 0.5 → 16 × 0.866 ≈ 13.9 ≈ 14.

explanation: The ramp is the hypotenuse (16 ft). The horizontal distance is the side adjacent to the 60° angle at ground level.
CAH: cos(60°) = adjacent/hypotenuse → adjacent = hypotenuse × cos(60°).
Horizontal = 16 × 0.5 = 8 feet.
Trap B (16): the horizontal is never the full ramp length — that would require a 0° angle.
Trap C (32): dividing by cos finds a missing hypotenuse, but the hypotenuse (ramp) is already known.
Trap D (14): sin(60°) ≈ 0.866 gives the vertical height, not the horizontal distance.
Desmos: type cos(60)*16 → 8. ✓

problems.calculatorStrategy: use_desmos_graph — type 600/sin(30) into Desmos. Desmos returns 1200 instantly. Watch the operation: this is division, not multiplication.
problems.question: An airplane descends along a straight path that makes a 30° angle with the ground. The airplane needs to lose 600 feet of altitude before landing. Using sin(30°) = 0.5, what is the total distance, in feet, the airplane travels along its descent path?
explanation: The descent path is the hypotenuse (unknown). The altitude lost (600 ft) is the side opposite the 30° angle.
SOH: sin(30°) = opposite/hypotenuse → hypotenuse = opposite/sin(30°).
Distance = 600 ÷ 0.5 = 1200 feet.
This is the reverse of the typical side-finding problem: you have the opposite leg and want the hypotenuse, so you DIVIDE by sin.
Trap 300: multiplied instead of divided (600 × 0.5 = 300). Multiplying finds the opposite leg when the hypotenuse is known — here the hypotenuse is the unknown.
Trap 600: reported the altitude directly, ignoring the trigonometry entirely.
Desmos: type 600/sin(30) → 1200. ✓

problems.calculatorStrategy: use_desmos_graph — type tan(45)*60 + 10 into Desmos. Two operations in one expression; press Enter once.
problems.question: A photographer stands 60 feet from the base of a wall. Using tan(45°) = 1, he calculates the height of the top of the wall. The wall supports a flagpole that extends 10 feet above the top of the wall. What is the total height of the tip of the flagpole above the ground, in feet?

choices.label: B
choices.trap: forgot_step_2: found the wall height (60 ft) but forgot to add the flagpole height (10 ft).

choices.label: C
choices.trap: wrong_reference_distance: added 10 to the distance (60 + 10 = 70) and then misapplied tan: tan(45°) × 70 = 70, then added again for 80, or other arithmetic confusion.

choices.label: D
choices.trap: subtracted_instead_of_added: subtracted the flagpole height instead of adding: 60 − 10 = 50.

explanation: Step 1 — find the wall height using tan(45°).
The photographer is 60 feet from the base (adjacent). The wall height is opposite the 45° angle.
TOA: tan(45°) = opposite/adjacent = wall height/60 → wall height = 60 × tan(45°) = 60 × 1 = 60 feet.
Step 2 — add the flagpole.
Total height = wall height + flagpole = 60 + 10 = 70 feet.
Trap B (60): completed only step 1 — found the wall but ignored the flagpole.
Trap D (50): subtracted the flagpole from the wall height.
Desmos: type tan(45)*60 + 10 → 70. ✓
